title: Capstone: Build a Secure Internal DevOps Platform
description: Deploy a complete internal DevOps platform with GitLab, Jenkins, Docker registry, databases, monitoring, security, and backup. Prove production readiness.
briefing:
### Mission Objective
Your organization needs a self-hosted, air-gapped DevOps platform for internal use. You will deploy GitLab CE as the source control hub, Jenkins for CI/CD pipelines, Harbor as the private Docker registry, and PostgreSQL as the backing database. Nginx will serve as a reverse proxy with TLS termination. Prometheus and Grafana will provide full observability, a Wazuh agent will forward security logs, and automated backups with restic will ensure data durability. Finally, you must write a comprehensive runbook documenting every component, its configuration, and recovery procedures.

### Why This Matters
In production environments, companies often need to host their entire DevOps toolchain internally for security, compliance, or latency reasons. This capstone proves you can architect, deploy, secure, monitor, and document a complex multi-service platform — skills that directly translate to senior DevOps and Platform Engineering roles.

### Environment
- Image: ubuntu:22.04
- Tools: docker, docker-compose, nginx, postgresql, gitlab-ce, jenkins, harbor, prometheus, grafana, wazuh-agent, restic
- Login: root / ItLab2025!

### Architecture
- Nginx reverse proxy on port 80/443 routing to GitLab (8929), Jenkins (8080), Harbor (8443)
- PostgreSQL 15 on port 5432 serving GitLab and Harbor databases
- Prometheus scraping exporters on port 9090, Grafana on port 3000
- Wazuh agent forwarding to /var/log/syslog
- Restic backups to /backup repo with daily cron
- Firewall rules restricting access to management ports only

### Deliverables
1. All services running and accessible via Nginx reverse proxy
2. TLS certificates installed and serving encrypted traffic
3. Prometheus scraping all targets, Grafana showing live dashboards
4. Wazuh agent forwarding security logs
5. Automated backups verified with test restore
6. Comprehensive runbook covering installation, configuration, troubleshooting, and recovery

### Permissions & Access
- Container runs as root
- All services run as systemd units or Docker containers
- TLS certificates generated with self-signed CA
- Verification via curl, systemctl, and CLI tools
tasks: Create databases for GitLab and Harbor
Deploy GitLab CE via Docker Compose
Deploy Harbor registry via Docker Compose
Install and configure Nginx reverse proxy
Configure Nginx upstream blocks for all services
Install and configure Prometheus with node_exporter
Deploy Grafana and import dashboard templates
Set up automated restic backups with cron
Create monitoring alerting rules in Prometheus

title: Capstone: Production Kubernetes Cluster from Scratch
description: Build a 3-node Kubernetes cluster using kubeadm with networking, ingress, monitoring, logging, secrets management, and a production app with autoscaling.
briefing:
### Mission Objective
You are tasked with building a production-grade Kubernetes cluster from scratch using kubeadm on 3 nodes (1 control-plane + 2 workers). You will install Calico CNI for pod networking, deploy the NGINX Ingress Controller, configure cert-manager for TLS, set up the Prometheus Operator for monitoring, deploy Loki for log aggregation, implement Sealed Secrets for sensitive data, deploy a sample application with Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, and write a complete operational runbook.

### Why This Matters
Kubernetes is the industry standard for container orchestration, but most engineers only use managed services. Building a cluster from scratch — not just using EKS or GKE — demonstrates deep understanding of control plane components, networking, storage, and security. This capstone proves you can operate K8s at the infrastructure level, debug cluster issues, and understand what happens under the hood when things go wrong.

### Environment
- Image: ubuntu:22.04
- Tools: kubeadm, kubectl, kubelet, calico, nginx-ingress, cert-manager, prometheus-operator, loki, sealed-secrets
- Login: root / ItLab2025!

### Architecture
- 1 control-plane node (k8s-master)
- 2 worker nodes (k8s-worker1, k8s-worker2)
- Calico CNI for pod-to-pod networking
- NGINX Ingress on host port 80/443
- Prometheus Operator in monitoring namespace
- Loki in logging namespace
- Sealed Secrets controller in kube-system
- Sample app with HPA scaling 2-10 replicas

### Deliverables
1. 3-node cluster with all nodes in Ready state
2. Calico CNI providing pod-to-pod networking
3. NGINX Ingress routing external traffic to services
4. cert-manager automating TLS certificate management
5. Prometheus Operator collecting cluster and application metrics
6. Loki aggregating pod logs for search and analysis
7. Sealed Secrets encrypting sensitive configuration data
8. Sample app with working HPA scaling on CPU metrics
9. Complete operational runbook covering installation and troubleshooting

### Permissions & Access
- Container runs as root with sudo access
- kubectl configured for admin access
- All nodes communicate on internal network
- Verification via kubectl and curl

title: Capstone: SOC in a Box — Full Security Operations Center
description: Deploy a complete Security Operations Center with SIEM, IDS, case management, SOAR automation, and custom detection rules.
briefing:
### Mission Objective
Build a fully functional Security Operations Center from scratch. Deploy Wazuh as the SIEM for log collection and correlation, Suricata as the network IDS for traffic inspection, the ELK stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) for log aggregation and visualization, TheHive for incident case management, Cortex for observable analysis, and Shuffle as the SOAR automation engine. Configure Slack webhook alerts, write custom detection rules, and create an incident response playbook that ties everything together.

### Why This Matters
SOC analysts are in high demand across every industry. Organizations need security professionals who can build and operate monitoring infrastructure, not just use pre-configured tools. This capstone proves you can build and operate the entire security monitoring pipeline — from network traffic inspection through log correlation to automated incident response. You will understand how security tools integrate, how to write detection rules, and how to operationalize threat detection into repeatable playbooks.

### Environment
- Image: ubuntu:22.04
- Tools: wazuh-manager, suricata, elasticsearch, logstash, kibana, thehive, cortex, shuffle
- Login: root / ItLab2025!

### Architecture
- Wazuh manager on port 1514 (UDP) / 1515 (TCP)
- Suricata monitoring eth0 in IDS mode
- Elasticsearch on port 9200, Logstash on port 5044, Kibana on port 5601
- TheHive on port 9000, Cortex on port 9001
- Shuffle SOAR on port 3001
- Slack webhook for alert notifications

### Deliverables
1. Wazuh collecting and correlating logs from all sources
2. Suricata detecting network anomalies with custom rules
3. ELK stack visualizing security events in Kibana dashboards
4. TheHive managing incident cases with full lifecycle tracking
5. Cortex analyzing observables (IPs, hashes, domains)
6. Shuffle automating incident response playbooks
7. Slack receiving real-time security alerts
8. Documented incident response playbook with escalation procedures

### Permissions & Access
- Container runs as root
- Elasticsearch requires 4GB+ heap
- All services run as systemd units or Docker containers
- Verification via curl, systemctl, and API calls

Deploy Kibana and connect to Elasticsearch
Configure Wazuh to forward logs to Logstash

title: Capstone: Production Database Cluster with Automated Failover
description: Deploy a 3-node PostgreSQL cluster with Patroni high availability, HAProxy load balancing, pgBouncer pooling, automated backups, and monitoring.
briefing:
### Mission Objective
Build a production-grade PostgreSQL cluster that can survive node failures. Deploy 3 PostgreSQL nodes managed by Patroni for automatic failover, HAProxy as the connection load balancer with health checks, pgBouncer for connection pooling, automated backups using restic to a local repository, and Prometheus monitoring. You must verify that failover actually works by killing the primary and confirming the cluster promotes a new leader.

### Why This Matters
Database availability is critical for any production application. Downtime means lost revenue, lost customers, and lost trust. This capstone teaches you to build a highly available database cluster with automatic failover, connection pooling, and backup/recovery. You will understand how Patroni uses etcd for leader election, how HAProxy routes traffic based on health, and how pgBouncer manages connection limits. These skills are essential for Database Administrators and SREs managing mission-critical data stores.

### Environment
- Image: ubuntu:22.04
- Tools: postgresql-15, patroni, haproxy, pgbouncer, restic, prometheus, etcd
- Login: root / ItLab2025!

### Architecture
- 3 PostgreSQL nodes: pg1 (5432), pg2 (5433), pg3 (5434)
- Patroni managing failover via etcd on port 2379
- HAProxy on ports 5000 (read/write) and 5001 (read-only) with health checks
- pgBouncer on port 6432 pooling connections to HAProxy
- Restic backing up to /backup repo every hour via cron
- Prometheus scraping Patroni and PostgreSQL exporters

### Deliverables
1. 3-node PostgreSQL cluster with streaming replication
2. Patroni managing automatic failover via etcd
3. HAProxy load balancing with health checks and read/write split
4. pgBouncer pooling database connections
5. Automated backups with verified restore capability
6. Prometheus monitoring cluster health and replication lag
7. Verified failover — primary killed, new leader elected automatically
8. Application connectivity maintained during failover

### Permissions & Access
- Container runs as root
- PostgreSQL runs as postgres user
- Patroni manages postgres lifecycle
- Verification via psql, curl, and systemctl
tasks: Join secondary nodes to Patroni cluster
Install and configure HAProxy with health checks
Set up automated backups with restic
Configure cron job for hourly backups
Configure Prometheus to scrape all nodes

title: Capstone: Full-Stack Application Deployment Pipeline
description: Build a complete CI/CD pipeline with Gitea, Drone CI, Docker builds, Nginx reverse proxy, Node.js app, MongoDB, TLS, auto-deploy on push, health checks, and rollback.
briefing:
### Mission Objective
Construct a full-stack deployment pipeline from source control to production. Deploy Gitea as a self-hosted Git server, Drone CI for continuous integration, build Docker images on every push, deploy a Node.js application behind an Nginx reverse proxy with Let's Encrypt TLS, connect to MongoDB, implement health checks, and configure rollback capability. When a developer pushes to the repository, the entire pipeline must execute automatically.

### Why This Matters
The CI/CD pipeline is the backbone of modern software delivery. Teams that can deploy frequently and reliably have a massive competitive advantage. This capstone proves you can build the entire toolchain — from code commit through build, test, containerize, deploy, and verify. You will understand how all pieces connect: Git hooks triggering CI, CI building containers, containers deploying to production, and monitoring verifying health. When the pipeline breaks, you will know exactly where to look.

### Environment
- Image: ubuntu:22.04
- Tools: gitea, drone, docker, nginx, nodejs, mongodb, certbot
- Login: root / ItLab2025!

### Architecture
- Gitea on port 3000 (source control)
- Drone CI on port 8080 (CI/CD)
- MongoDB on port 27017 (application database)
- Node.js app on port 4000 (application)
- Nginx on port 80/443 (reverse proxy with TLS)
- Docker registry local on port 5000

### Deliverables
1. Gitea hosting the application repository with admin user
2. Drone CI building Docker images on every push
3. Node.js application deployed and responding to requests
4. Nginx reverse proxy with TLS termination
5. MongoDB connected and serving application data
6. Health check endpoint returning 200 OK status
7. Rollback capability verified by reverting a commit
8. End-to-end pipeline: push → build → deploy → verify

### Permissions & Access
- Container runs as root
- Gitea admin: admin / ItLab2025!
- Drone admin: admin / ItLab2025!
- MongoDB no auth for lab purposes
- Verification via curl, docker, and systemctl

title: Capstone: Enterprise Monitoring Stack
description: Deploy a full observability platform with Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, Loki, Jaeger, custom exporters, and multi-host monitoring.
briefing:
### Mission Objective
Build an enterprise-grade monitoring and observability stack. Deploy Prometheus for metrics collection across multiple targets, Grafana for visualization with pre-built dashboards, Alertmanager for alert routing with Slack integration, Loki for log aggregation, Jaeger for distributed tracing, node_exporter on multiple simulated hosts, custom application exporters, and proper alert routing with escalation policies.

### Why This Matters
You cannot manage what you cannot measure. In production environments, understanding system health requires three pillars of observability: metrics (what is happening now), logs (what happened), and traces (how requests flow through services). This capstone proves you can build all three into a unified platform. SREs and Platform Engineers use these skills daily to ensure system reliability, optimize performance, and respond rapidly to incidents before they impact users.

### Environment
- Image: ubuntu:22.04
- Tools: prometheus, grafana, alertmanager, loki, jaeger, node-exporter, custom-exporters
- Login: root / ItLab2025!

### Architecture
- Prometheus on port 9090 scraping targets every 15s
- Grafana on port 3000 with Prometheus and Loki datasources
- Alertmanager on port 9093 routing to Slack webhook
- Loki on port 3100 for log aggregation
- Jaeger on port 16686 for trace visualization
- node_exporter on ports 9100, 9101, 9102 (3 simulated hosts)
- Custom app exporter on port 9103

### Deliverables
1. Prometheus scraping all 5+ targets successfully
2. Grafana with pre-built dashboards showing live data
3. Alertmanager routing alerts to Slack channel
4. Loki ingesting and querying application logs
5. Jaeger visualizing distributed traces across services
6. Custom exporter exposing application-specific metrics
7. Alert rules triggering on CPU, memory, and disk thresholds
8. End-to-end observability: metric → alert → notification

### Permissions & Access
- Container runs as root
- All services run as systemd units
- Grafana admin: admin / admin
- Verification via curl, promtool, and systemctl
tasks: Configure Prometheus scrape targets for 3 hosts
Import Grafana dashboard for node metrics
Create alerting rules for CPU, memory, disk

title: Capstone: Microservices Platform with Service Mesh
description: Deploy a microservices platform on K3s with Istio service mesh, mTLS, traffic management, circuit breaking, observability, and canary deployments.
briefing:
### Mission Objective
Build a production microservices platform using K3s as the lightweight Kubernetes distribution and Istio as the service mesh. Deploy 3 interconnected microservices (API gateway, user service, order service), enable mutual TLS for all service-to-service communication, configure traffic management with canary deployments, implement circuit breaker patterns, set up Prometheus and Grafana for mesh observability, configure Jaeger for distributed tracing, and perform a live canary deployment shifting traffic from v1 to v2.

### Why This Matters
Microservices and service meshes are the architecture of choice for modern cloud-native applications. A service mesh handles cross-cutting concerns like security (mTLS), traffic management (canary deployments, retries), and observability (traces, metrics) at the infrastructure level. This capstone proves you can deploy, configure, and operate a service mesh with advanced traffic management. You will understand mTLS encryption, circuit breaker patterns, traffic shifting, and distributed tracing — skills that distinguish senior platform engineers from juniors.

### Environment
- Image: ubuntu:22.04
- Tools: k3s, istio, kubectl, helm, prometheus, grafana, jaeger
- Login: root / ItLab2025!

### Architecture
- K3s single-node cluster
- Istio service mesh with sidecar injection
- 3 microservices: api-gateway, user-service, order-service
- mTLS strict mode across all namespaces
- VirtualService for traffic splitting (90/10 canary)
- DestinationRule with circuit breaker
- Prometheus + Grafana for Istio metrics
- Jaeger for distributed tracing

### Deliverables
1. K3s cluster running with all nodes Ready
2. Istio installed with sidecar injection enabled
3. 3 microservices deployed with Istio sidecars attached
4. Strict mTLS enforced across all services
5. VirtualService splitting traffic 90/10 for canary
6. DestinationRule with circuit breaker configured
7. Prometheus and Grafana showing Istio metrics
8. Jaeger visualizing distributed traces across services
9. Live canary deployment from v1 to v2 with traffic shift

### Permissions & Access
- Container runs as root
- kubectl configured for K3s
- Istio CLI (istioctl) available
- Verification via kubectl, istioctl, and curl

Deploy Prometheus and Grafana for Istio

title: Capstone: Disaster Recovery & Business Continuity Lab
description: Build a PostgreSQL primary-replica setup with automated backups, verify failover, test restore from backup, measure RTO/RPO, and run a full DR drill.
briefing:
### Mission Objective
Implement a complete disaster recovery strategy for a PostgreSQL database. Deploy a primary-replica streaming replication setup, configure automated backups with restic to a local repository, test restoring from backup, measure Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO), perform failover testing, document all DR procedures in a runbook, and execute a full DR drill simulating a complete primary failure.

### Why This Matters
Disaster recovery is not optional — it is a business requirement. Every production database needs a tested backup and recovery strategy. This capstone proves you can design, implement, and test a DR strategy for a production database. You will learn to measure RTO/RPO, verify backup integrity, perform failover drills, and document procedures that operations teams can follow under pressure. The ability to recover from data loss or infrastructure failure is what separates junior from senior operations engineers.

### Environment
- Image: ubuntu:22.04
- Tools: postgresql-15, restic, pg_basebackup, wal-g, cron
- Login: root / ItLab2025!

### Architecture
- PostgreSQL primary on port 5432
- PostgreSQL replica on port 5433 with streaming replication
- Restic backup repository at /backup
- WAL archiving to /var/lib/postgresql/wal_archive
- Cron jobs for automated backups every 30 minutes
- DR runbook at /home/student/dr-runbook.md

### Deliverables
1. Primary-replica streaming replication verified with pg_stat_replication
2. Automated backups running every 30 minutes via cron
3. Verified restore from backup to alternate location
4. RTO measured and documented (target: under 5 minutes)
5. RPO measured and documented (target: under 30 minutes)
6. Failover tested — primary killed, replica promoted to primary
7. Complete DR runbook with step-by-step recovery procedures
8. DR drill executed and results documented with timestamps

### Permissions & Access
- Container runs as root
- PostgreSQL runs as postgres user
- Primary and replica on same host (different ports)
- Verification via psql, pg_isready, and restic
tasks: Create replication user and configure pg_hba.conf

title: Capstone: Production Mail Server Stack
description: Deploy a complete mail server with Postfix SMTP, Dovecot IMAP, Rspamd anti-spam, DKIM, SPF, DMARC, TLS, Roundcube webmail, and mail client testing.
briefing:
### Mission Objective
Build a fully functional production mail server from scratch. Deploy Postfix for SMTP sending and receiving, Dovecot for IMAP/POP3 access, Rspamd for intelligent spam filtering, configure DKIM signing for email authentication, set up SPF and DMARC DNS records, generate TLS certificates, deploy Roundcube as a webmail client, and test end-to-end mail flow from sending through spam filtering to delivery.

### Why This Matters
Email infrastructure is the backbone of business communication. Self-hosting a mail server teaches you SMTP, IMAP, DNS authentication (DKIM/SPF/DMARC), spam filtering, TLS, and web application deployment. Understanding how email works at the protocol level — from message composition through DNS lookup, DKIM verification, spam scoring, and delivery — is invaluable for system administrators, DevOps engineers, and security professionals managing communication infrastructure.

### Environment
- Image: ubuntu:22.04
- Tools: postfix, dovecot, rspamd, opendkim, roundcube, certbot
- Login: root / ItLab2025!

### Architecture
- Postfix SMTP on port 25 (incoming), 587 (submission), 465 (SMTPS)
- Dovecot IMAP on port 143 (IMAP), 993 (IMAPS), 110 (POP3), 995 (POP3S)
- Rspamd on port 11332 (control), 11333 (normal)
- OpenDKIM on port 8891
- Roundcube webmail on port 9090
- TLS certificates for all services

### Deliverables
1. Postfix accepting and delivering email on port 25
2. Dovecot providing IMAP access with TLS encryption
3. Rspamd filtering spam with bayesian learning capability
4. DKIM signing all outgoing mail with valid signatures
5. SPF and DMARC records configured for domain authentication
6. TLS certificates installed on all services
7. Roundcube webmail accessible and functional
8. End-to-end mail flow verified: send → filter → deliver → read

### Permissions & Access
- Container runs as root
- Postfix runs as postfix user
- Mailboxes at /var/mail/
- DKIM keys at /etc/opendkim/keys/
- Verification via telnet, curl, and doveadm

title: Capstone: Edge Computing Platform
description: Deploy K3s at the edge with MQTT broker, Node-RED for processing, Prometheus monitoring, device simulation, data pipeline, and OTA updates.
briefing:
### Mission Objective
Build an edge computing platform that processes IoT data locally before sending it to a central database. Deploy K3s as the edge Kubernetes distribution, Mosquitto as the MQTT message broker, Node-RED for visual data flow processing, Prometheus for edge monitoring, simulate IoT devices publishing sensor data, build a data pipeline from MQTT through Node-RED to a PostgreSQL central database, and implement OTA (Over-The-Air) update capability for edge applications.

### Why This Matters
Edge computing is transforming industries from manufacturing to smart cities. Processing data locally reduces latency, saves bandwidth, and enables real-time decision making. This capstone proves you can deploy and manage edge infrastructure that processes data locally, communicates via MQTT (the standard IoT protocol), and synchronizes with central systems. These skills are critical for IoT architects, embedded platform engineers, and anyone building distributed systems that span cloud and edge.

### Environment
- Image: ubuntu:22.04
- Tools: k3s, mosquitto, nodered, prometheus, node-exporter, postgresql
- Login: root / ItLab2025!

### Architecture
- K3s running on edge node
- Mosquitto MQTT broker on port 1883 (MQTT), 9001 (WebSocket)
- Node-RED on port 1880 for data processing
- Prometheus on port 9090 scraping edge metrics
- PostgreSQL on port 5432 as central data store
- IoT simulator publishing temperature/humidity data
- OTA update controller in K3s

### Deliverables
1. K3s running edge workloads in Kubernetes pods
2. Mosquitto MQTT broker handling sensor messages reliably
3. Node-RED processing and transforming incoming data
4. PostgreSQL storing sensor readings in structured tables
5. Prometheus monitoring edge node health and resource usage
6. IoT simulator generating realistic temperature/humidity data
7. Data pipeline flowing: device → MQTT → Node-RED → PostgreSQL
8. OTA update mechanism for deploying edge application changes

### Permissions & Access
- Container runs as root
- K3s manages edge workloads
- MQTT broker accepts anonymous connections for lab
- Verification via mosquitto_pub, curl, and psql
tasks: Install and configure K3s for edge
Install and configure Mosquitto MQTT broker
Create data processing flow in Node-RED
Create database schema for sensor data
Build MQTT to PostgreSQL data pipeline
Verify data flows to central database
